passage: So Reena, you know how it went behind the canteen? Six of us, and Tamanna announces we should skip science and watch the match at the tea stall. Everyone was hyped. I just said, "Nah, not for me, have fun though," in a light way, no speech. Two people rolled their eyes, and Tamanna said, "Your loss." My face went hot. Then you said, "Actually, I'm heading to class too," and we walked off together. I have never been so grateful for one person. We sat in the back row and laughed at how nervous we both were. On Monday the group was fine with me, mostly. Not bad for Seema, right?

qa.q: What did Tamanna suggest the group do?
qa.a: Tamanna suggested they skip science and watch the match at the tea stall.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling after Reena said "Actually, I'm heading to class too"?
qa.a: Seema felt grateful and relieved; having one person who agreed made the refusal far easier to keep than saying no alone.

qa.q: What made Seema's refusal work without a fight?
qa.a: Seema kept it light and short, "Nah, not for me, have fun though", with no lecture, and accepted one ally instead of arguing.

qa.q: How might Reena have felt before speaking up after Seema's refusal?
qa.a: Reena may have felt just as nervous as Seema and been waiting for someone else to say no first; the shared laughing later suggests the nervousness was mutual.

grounding: A teenager says a relaxed no without a lecture, and one ally who feels the same makes dissent easy to sustain.

passage: I was in the bunk above Leela's on the school trip, so I saw the whole thing. Around ten, four boys from the next room knocked and said they were sneaking out to wander the town. Wasim was on the floor with a book. He said, "Not for me, thanks, I'm going to sleep," smiling, like he was declining an extra biscuit. Someone said "boring". Wasim just shrugged. Then Leela said from her bunk, "Same, honestly," and Wasim looked up and grinned. The boys left. I said nothing, but I lay there thinking Wasim seemed calm, and a lot less lonely once Leela spoke.

qa.q: Where were the four boys planning to go?
qa.a: The four boys were sneaking out to wander the town.

qa.q: What does Wasim's smile while declining suggest about how Wasim feels?
qa.a: The smile and shrug suggest Wasim feels calm and comfortable refusing, and the grin at Leela's "Same, honestly" shows relief and gratitude at having an ally.

qa.q: How could the person on the top bunk support Wasim and Leela next time?
qa.a: The narrator could speak up too, saying "same" out loud, since each extra voice makes dissent easier and less lonely.

qa.q: What might Leela have felt when saying "Same, honestly" from the bunk?
qa.a: Leela may have wanted to back Wasim and to avoid being seen as boring, and speaking from the bunk suggests a small, easy way to join without any drama.

grounding: A teenager gives a relaxed no thanks, not for me, and a second person's agreement makes dissent easier, told through an observer.

passage:
Tuesday: Behind the tuition building, Ritu held out a cigarette. “Just one puff, Jaya.” Four girls watched. Jaya shrugged. “Nah, not for me,” she said, and kept eating her chips. It was quiet for a second, awkward.
Friday: Same corner. Ritu offered again. Urmila, the new girl, said, “Me neither, actually,” and sat next to Jaya. The two of them split a packet of peanuts and talked about the physics test. Nobody pushed.
Two weeks later: When the cigarette came round, Jaya didn't even have to answer. Urmila said, “We're good,” and Ritu nodded and moved on. Walking home, Jaya realised her hands hadn't shaken once.

qa.q: What did Jaya say the first time Ritu offered?
qa.a: She said, "Nah, not for me."

qa.q: How did Jaya's feelings change from Tuesday to two weeks later?
qa.a: At first she felt awkward and tense in the quiet, but with Urmila beside her she felt calm and steady, and her hands didn't shake once.

qa.q: Which part of Jaya's refusal worked, and why?
qa.a: She said no lightly and kept eating without lecturing anyone, so nobody felt judged and there was little to argue with.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Urmila to speak up on Friday?
qa.a: As the new girl she may have been nervous, and seeing Jaya refuse first probably gave her the courage to join.

grounding: Shows a teenager giving a relaxed no without a lecture and finding one ally, which makes refusing much easier over time.

passage:
Nikita beta, you think you're the only one who gets pushed? Let me tell you, this is Nazia khala speaking from experience.
When I was fifteen, the girls in my class had a plan: copy the geography answers off a leaked paper. Shabnam waved it at us behind the water tank. “Everyone's seen it, Nazia.”
I didn't give a speech. I just said, “No thanks, I'll take my chances,” and went back to learning my maps.
I thought I'd be alone for the whole term. But that evening Rekha came to my house with her atlas. “Can we study together? I didn't look either.” We quizzed each other till the lamp oil ran low. That one friend made the whole thing feel easy.

qa.q: What did Shabnam wave behind the water tank?
qa.a: She waved a leaked geography paper.

qa.q: What was young Nazia expecting to feel after saying no?
qa.a: She expected to feel lonely for the whole term, alone because she refused.

qa.q: What turning point in the story made Nazia's refusal easier to keep?
qa.a: Rekha coming to her house with an atlas; having one friend who also refused turned a lonely choice into a shared one.

qa.q: How might Rekha have felt going to Nazia's house that evening?
qa.a: She may have felt nervous but relieved to find someone else who didn't look, and grateful not to study alone.

grounding: An elder recalls giving a relaxed no to cheating without a lecture and finding one friend who felt the same, which made dissent easier.

passage:
The school trip bus had broken down outside Nashik, and the rain was coming sideways. Ms Rao had forty students to count under one petrol-station shelter.
“She won't notice,” Kunal whispered. “The market's right there. Five minutes for pakoras. Everyone's going.”
Seven kids began edging towards the road. Vandana pulled her hood up. “Nah, I'm staying dry. Not for me.”
“Boring,” said Kunal.
Himani, beside her, let out a breath. “Same, honestly.”
The group hesitated. Two of them came back and stood with the girls. Ms Rao counted again, frowning, and got thirty-eight. Kunal's group came running back, soaked. Himani nudged Vandana, and both of them tried very hard not to laugh.

qa.q: Where did the bus break down?
qa.a: It broke down outside Nashik.

qa.q: How did Himani seem to feel when Vandana spoke up?
qa.a: She seemed relieved; she let out a breath and said "Same, honestly," glad not to be the only one staying.

qa.q: What made Vandana's refusal work well?
qa.a: It was short and relaxed, with no lecture, so it didn't insult anyone and even made two others feel free to come back.

qa.q: What might Ms Rao be feeling when she counted thirty-eight?
qa.a: She was probably worried and frustrated, since two students were missing in the rain while she was responsible for all forty.

grounding: Shows a teenager saying a relaxed no without lecturing and gaining one ally, after which others find it easier to stay too.

passage: On the society terrace after the Class 11 farewell, someone produced a cigarette and passed it round the circle of eight. When it reached Pankaj, he just smiled and said, 'Nah, I'm good,' and passed it on. No speech. A couple of boys said, 'Ooh, good boy,' and laughed. Pankaj shrugged and went back to his cold drink. Ujjwal, next in line, looked at the cigarette, then at Pankaj. 'Same. I'm good too.' The teasing lasted maybe ten seconds before the talk moved on to cricket. Later, walking home, Ujjwal said, 'I've been wanting to say no for months. Didn't want to be the only one.' Pankaj grinned. 'Now there's two of us.'

qa.q: What did Pankaj say when the cigarette reached him?
qa.a: 'Nah, I'm good.'

qa.q: What had Ujjwal been feeling before that night?
qa.a: Ujjwal had wanted to refuse for months but felt afraid of being the only one.

qa.q: What made Pankaj's refusal work?
qa.a: It was relaxed and short, with no lecture, so the teasing faded fast and Ujjwal felt able to join in.

qa.q: How might the boys who teased Pankaj see the moment later?
qa.a: They may have forgotten it quickly, since there was no lecture to react to and the talk moved on to cricket.

grounding: A teenager refuses lightly, without a lecture, and one friend joins him, making it far easier to hold out.
